implementation_notes: Swift exposes laziness as a sequence view: .lazy returns a sequence on which operations such as map and filter are implemented lazily (Apple's LazySequenceProtocol documentation), so the adapters apply per element when the result is iterated, and concrete lazy types (LazyMapSequence/LazyFilterSequence) compose without materializing. sequence(first:next:)/sequence(state:next:)/AnySequence build lazy sequences from closures, and lazy views are not memoized - a second iteration recomputes, so cache with Array(...) when elements are expensive.
pitfalls: Swift's lazy view does not memoize: iterating a lazy sequence twice repeats all element work; materialize (Array(...)) if the result is reused.

A lazy view captures and retains the base sequence, so holding a lazy sequence over a huge collection keeps that collection alive, and sequence(state:next:) closures are single-use with inout state that must not escape.

Lazy adapters are value types, but a closure that captures a class with mutable shared state is not thread-safe; lazy sequences also cannot be used where a random-access collection is required (indexing/SubSequence operations).

variants.name: AsyncSequence / AsyncStream (Swift 5.5)
variants.idiom_name: AsyncSequence with for await / AsyncStream builder
variants.implementation_notes: For element production that awaits, Swift's counterpart is AsyncSequence: a sequence whose iterator's next() is async, consumed with for await in an async context, and built from AsyncStream/AsyncThrowingStream, AsyncSequence adapters (map/filter/prefix) or an async-returning sequence factory. It replaces the synchronous lazy view when each element needs awaited I/O or a callback source needs bridging; cancellation propagates through the task, so the consumer must still close or cancel the stream explicitly when it stops early.
variants.code_sketch:
let lines = AsyncStream<String> { continuation in
    let handle = openSource { line in continuation.yield(line) }   // bridged callback
    continuation.onTermination = { _ in handle.cancel() }          // cleanup hook
}

for await line in lines {                 // one awaited element per iteration
    if line.contains("ERROR") { break }    // termination handler runs
}
pitfalls: AsyncSequence elements arrive from a task: abandoning for await without cancelling the task (or triggering onTermination) leaves the producer running.
An AsyncStream buffers by default (unbounded buffering with .unbounded policy) unless a buffering policy is supplied, so a slow consumer can grow memory instead of applying backpressure.
Async sequences cannot be iterated twice and their adapters are not memoized - a second pass over the same sequence may be empty or restart the work depending on the source.
